text.en: An art group wants enough coloured pencils for a workshop. Nila wonders how many pencils students usually bring. She plans a fair way to ask.

A statistical question expects answers that can vary. Decide whom to ask, which quantity to collect and which units to use. A statement describes the answers collected. State the group the results came from before using them to make wider claims.
Asking how many pencils each student brought can give different numbers. These answers form a data set.
Say who will be counted and what each number measures. Use pencils per student for this survey.
If most answers are between four and six pencils, we can describe that pattern for the group we actually surveyed.
A result from six students does not show what every student in the school usually brings.

board.text: Test the scope of a claim

problem.en: Which question is statistical: How many pencils did Anu bring today, or how many did each of the six students bring today?

text.en: Anu’s count is a single fixed answer.

why.en: It asks about one person in one situation.

text.en: The six counts may differ, so the second question is statistical.

why.en: Collect answers for everyone in the named group.

prompt.en: Turn a question about one student’s reading time into a statistical question.

requiredIdeas.en: Ask the same reading-time question of a named group.
Use a shared time period and unit.

points.en: Describe the group and units when reporting results.
